articles.title: Democrat Josh Turek wins Iowa Senate race
articles.summary: Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa Senate race, CBS News projects, in a major pickup for Democrats as they seek to...
articles.body:
Washington — Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa Senate race, CBS News projects, in a major pickup for Democrats as they seek to take control of the upper chamber.

Turek, 47, is a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian and state representative who campaigned on his record of working across the aisle, and sought what was initially viewed as a long-shot bid for the seat in the U.S Senate after GOP Sen. Joni Ernst announced she wouldn't seek reelection.

But the race proved more competitive than expected, despite the state's rightward shift in recent years, as the Trump administration's trade policies, the unpopular war in Iran and high gas and diesel prices hit Iowans especially hard.

Hinson, 43, is a former local news anchor who has represented Iowa in the House since 2021 and initially vowed to be President Trump's "top ally" in the Senate. Hinson had to tread a fine line as she pitched her candidacy in the Hawkeye State. In the weeks ahead of the election, Hinson called for the war to be brought to a "successful and immediate end," though she had opposed efforts in Congress to rein in the president's war powers. And during a debate in October, while she said she'll be the president's ally when it's "important for Iowa," she also pledged to "push back on him."

In the leadup to election day, polls showed Hinson and Turek locked in a tight race, forcing both sides to spend heavily in the state.

Once a swing state, Iowa hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, and Mr. Trump won the state by 13 points in 2024.

The projected victory brought Democrats a fifth flip, giving them enough seats to secure a majority. Despite a map that had initially looked favorable to Republicans, steep headwinds emerged for the party as competitive races cropped up in reliably red states like Iowa in recent months, throwing the GOP's hold on the upper chamber into question.

Democrat Rob Sand won the governor's race in Iowa.

articles.title: Michigan U.S. Senate race between El-Sayed, Rogers too close to call
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – The Michigan U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – The Michigan U.S. Senate race between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is too close to call, with votes still being counted in one of the nation's most closely watched contests.

El-Sayed and Rogers remain locked in a tight contest. Michigan has not elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate since 1994, and Rogers also lost his bid for the seat in 2024.

With 48% of precincts reporting at midnight, El-Sayed was leading 50.3%-47.8%, with more than 2.4 million votes counted.

The winner will succeed Democratic U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, who was first elected in 2014. Peters announced in January 2025 that he would not seek reelection.

The race between El-Sayed and Rogers was particularly heated and was considered one of the nation's most consequential U.S. Senate contests, with control of the 120th Congress hanging in the balance.

Democrats were divided during the primary between El-Sayed and establishment-backed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens. El-Sayed, who is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, narrowly defeated Stevens.

Following the primary, much of the Democratic establishment rallied behind the 41-year-old El-Sayed. Former President Barack Obama campaigned alongside him in Detroit. However, Stevens broke with her party's nominee, endorsing Rogers in the final days of the campaign.

Going into election night, El-Sayed was leading Rogers in the polls by upwards of 6%, generally outside the margin of error.

In 2024, Michigan's U.S. Senate race was decided by less than half a percentage point, with Democrat Elissa Slotkin narrowly defeating Rogers. Rogers returned as the Republican nominee in 2026 after securing the party's nomination unopposed.

El-Sayed is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. He has cast himself as a progressive and faced repeated allegations of extremism throughout his campaign. During a weekend rally, Trump called him a "jihadist" and said he was "on the side of the terrorists."

The 41-year-old responded to the president's frequent attacks on the campaign trail.

"I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November," El-Sayed said during a rally Sunday. "I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro."

articles.title: Democrat Annie Andrews wins South Carolina Senate race
articles.summary: Democrat Annie Andrews won a stunning upset over GOP Sen. Darline Graham, who was running for her late brother Lindsey Graham's seat.
articles.body:
Washington — Democrat Annie Andrews defeated GOP Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race, CBS News projects, in a major upset.

Andrews, 45, is a pediatrician and campaigned on healthcare access and affordability, along with fighting corruption in Washington. She faced off against Graham, the incumbent senator who was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother Lindsey Graham's term after his sudden death in July.

Darline Graham, 62, most recently served as commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, before she was appointed to the Senate. She went on to win a special primary election to take her brother's place on the ballot to represent South Carolina for a full six-year term.

Andrews faced an uphill battle in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998, and which President Trump won by 18 points in 2024. She criticized Darline Graham for lacking experience, pointing to comments she made during the condensed primary, when she said she was "not that informed on national security."

The race, which grew much more competitive than expected, forced Republicans to come to Graham's aid with a $5 million investment in October from the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican super PAC. MAGA Inc., a super PAC controlled by Mr. Trump, also gave Graham $827,000 in August, and he personally campaigned heavily for Graham after encouraging her to run for the seat. But the efforts fell short amid a difficult environment for Republicans.

With Andrews' projected victory, Democrats secured an unexpected pickup, helping to propel them to a majority.

articles.title: ‘Buckle up’: A defiant White House pins blame elsewhere
articles.summary: Tonight’s elections are a repudiation of Republicans that some in the White House have been unwilling to own.
articles.body:
The White House began Tuesday night with cautious optimism. As Democrats started racking up victories, President Donald Trump's advisers grew more candid — and defiant.

Trump spent the weeks before the midterms traveling across the country, hosting 30 events across 20 states in just over a month as he urged voters to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." What resulted was a midterm repudiation of Republicans that, as election night wore on, some in the White House were unwilling to own.

"President Trump was not on the ballot, and it's proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot," a White House official told Semafor, arguing that he "did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves."

Trump himself echoed the sentiment in a Tuesday night social media post : "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

The early results on Tuesday night made clear that Trump's aggressive campaign push wasn't enough to surmount public frustration with the Iran war and his tariffs' effect on the cost of living. Democrats quickly flipped North Carolina, held onto New Hampshire and Georgia — and then flipped long-scarlet South Carolina. Trump officials and people close to the White House quickly acknowledged that a massive blue wave was coming.

One Trump administration official emphasized how much the war has directly affected Americans. That conflict amplified voters' frustration as gas prices climbed, and many in Trump's base felt betrayed by a president who'd campaigned on launching no new wars.

Another Trump ally went even further, describing the war as a "disaster" and lamenting that "the Republican party doesn't understand the Trump coalition, even though it's 10 years in."

Officials' efforts to pin their stunning midterm setback on other GOP leaders suggest that the White House has no plans to seek conciliation with ascendant congressional Democratic majorities.

"Regardless of how today plays out, President Trump's resolve to stop the Radical Left is only going to become stronger," the White House official added. "Buckle up."

Trump told The New York Times late Tuesday that he would accept the results of the election.

In the past few weeks, some administration officials have begun looking to hire lawyers to preempt Democrat-led investigations — an early sign that they knew Tuesday night's results might not go their way. To that point, some advisers indicated to Semafor that the results rolling in so far were not surprising to them. Trump has often pointed over the past months to historical data showing that the party holding total control of Washington tends to perform poorly in midterm elections.

Even before polls across the country closed, the White House began circulating talking points highlighting Trump's efforts on the trail. That underlying message — that the president did what he could to help — largely persisted inside the administration as the losses mounted. One adviser told Semafor that Trump's thinking remains along those lines: that he did what he could.

Several Trump allies also argued to Semafor that poor candidate quality was partly to blame for Republican defeats, though the president openly endorsed several of the candidates who fell short.

Trump certainly made himself a central figure in Tuesday's election. Democrats looked to amplify his calls for voters to pretend he was on the ballot, believing that voters were so dissatisfied with the administration that a midterm referendum on Trump would reward them.

Trump watched the election results roll in from the White House East Room alongside Cabinet members, senior staff, and political advisers, another White House official told Semafor. At times, he took to Truth Social to rage against Fox News' coverage of the evening.

Some staffers ordered in from the Cheesecake Factory, an apparent nod to the now-famous quip from former President Barack Obama about Trump's decorating.

Tonight's results are a warning sign for the Republican Party as it tries to look past Trump. And they're likely to surface a question that some of his aides knew they'd inevitably face: whether the coalition that pushed Trump to power can be reconstituted, and what the party will stand for after Trump leaves office.

Some Republicans I've texted with tonight are already confronting that question. In the weeks and months ahead, anyone in the GOP who's eyeing a 2028 run will need to look at the midterm results and find ways to run with a different message than Trump — while not angering him or his base.

articles.title: Troy Jackson defeats Susan Collins to flip Maine Senate seat for Dems
articles.summary: Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated Susan Collins, a five-term incumbent and the last Republican senator left in New England.
articles.body:
Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, flipping a long Republican-held seat and giving his party a crucial win as they seek to flip the U.S. Senate, according to projections by CNN and Fox News .

Collins called her opponent to concede, Jackson campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad confirmed to USA TODAY.

Jackson had just a few months to run his Senate campaign after oyster farmer Graham Platner dropped out of the race following accusations of sexual assault, which he denies. Platner's charisma and anti-establishment messaging had inspired a grassroots movement that helped him overtake Maine's Democratic Gov. Janet Mills in the Democratic primary.

Platner's exit from the race prompted worries about the Democrats' chances of defeating Collins, who has been in office for 30 years and is the only Republican to represent a state won by Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. The race remained in a dead heat through much of the year, according to polls.

But many remained committed to the movement and Jackson, a logger who served as state Senate president for six years, was also seen as an ideologically similar champion for economic populist policies—if less charismatic and sometimes emotional . While he started his career as a Republican who opposed abortion and gay marriage, he is now a progressive Democrat who has received high scores from abortion and LGBTQ groups . As a state legislator, he cosponsored Maine's expanded abortion rights protection and passed legislation giving loggers and haulers the right to unionize .

Throughout the campaign, Jackson highlighted his progressive bonafides, campaigning with heavy weights like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Verment, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, while tying Collins to President Donald Trump .

Collins has long held a reputation as a moderate Republican who has brought a lot of money back for Maine, and those are the arguments she leaned on in her campaign. But that reputation has been harder to uphold in the Trump era, where Mainers increasingly saw her as not doing enough to stop Trump's agenda. According to an October Marist poll , 59% of Maine voters disapproved of the president.

See Susan Collins, Troy Jackson and more campaign in Maine midterms

An Oct. 1 analysis of the majority of Trump's second term from CQ Roll Call found Collins voted with the president 92% of the time. A New York Times analysis of her voting record found that her opposing votes rarely stopped Trump's agenda from passing. In one debate where Collins was asked for an example in which she voted against her party and actually changed the outcome, she touted her vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – but Hegseth was ultimately confirmed.

In an interview before the election, University of Maine Farmington political science professor Jim Melcher told USA TODAY that Trump, in some ways, has been "the absolute worst thing that could have happened to Susan Collins."

articles.title: Jon Ossoff wins Georgia Senate race, keeping seat for Democrats
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defeated GOP Rep. Mike Collins in the Georgia Senate race, CBS News projects, holding onto his seat in the upper chamber.
articles.body:
Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defeated GOP Rep. Mike Collins in the Georgia Senate race, CBS News projects, holding onto his seat in the upper chamber.

Ossoff, 39, was the sole Democrat seeking reelection in a state that President Trump won in 2024. He first came to the Senate in 2021, when he delivered Democrats one of two runoff victories in Georgia. This cycle, Republicans saw the race as a key prize as they sought to keep control of the chamber. But after a messy primary fight, and facing personal controversies and national headwinds, Collins was unable to make significant inroads in the Peach State.

Collins, 59, prevailed during the primary, becoming the Republican nominee in June after a runoff. The owner of a trucking business, Collins has represented Georgia in the House since 2023, and attempted to cast Ossoff as out of touch with Georgian values. But his campaign was beset by questions about people in Collins' circle, including a former staffer who reportedly shared Nazi and KKK images on social media.

Although the race was once viewed as the easiest pickup opportunity for Republicans, as Georgia shifted toward the right during the last election, Collins' closeness to the president was seen as a boon for Ossoff, who has also been a formidable fundraiser. Heading into election night, Ossoff was leading in the polls.

With the projected victory, Democrats retained a key seat, helping to cement their majority.

articles.title: Science is moving beyond animal testing. Why is India going backwards?
articles.summary: Using animal biology to model human disease has long reached its scientific and moral limits.
articles.body: Using animal biology to model human disease has long reached its scientific and moral limits. Worldwide, progressive regulators are replacing animal experimentation with human-relevant methods that deliver faster, more reliable safety data. But India is poised to weaken statutory protections and lower ethical standards it has, ironically, demonstrated leadership in.At the centre of this regressive shift is the draft Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Control and Supervision of Experiments, Breeding and Trading of Laboratory Animals) Rules 2026. Issued by Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA) under fisheries, animal husbandry and dairying ministry, the proposed text seeks to replace foundational frameworks established in 1968 and 1998.

articles.title: Lone Star turns blue: Democrats Talarico, Hinojosa topple Texas Republicans
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminarian who campaigned on a "politics of love," on Tuesday won the US Senate race in Texa...
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminarian who campaigned on a "politics of love," on Tuesday won the US Senate race in Texas, dealing a historic blow to Republicans that could reshape American politics.

Talarico defeated the state's attorney general Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who was heavily backed by tech billionaire Elon Musk, US media projected.

The result was a major setback for Trump, who threw his weight behind Paxton and made the state a campaign priority.

"We defeated Goliath," Talarico told a victory rally in Austin, the state capital.

"In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington, DC establishment," he said.

Talarico took aim at billionaires "who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens" and who "want us at each other's throats."

In another political earthquake for the deeply conservative southern border state, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

Talarico and Hinojosa are the first Democrats to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.

Hinojosa, a 52-year-old attorney and state lawmaker, is part of a new generation of Democrats who are seeking to attract independents and voters disillusioned by Trump's unpopular war in the Middle East and skyrocketing prices for gas and everyday goods.

Thousands of supporters gathered at a watch party in Austin erupted in joy as the results came in, many of them crying and hugging.

Some chanted "Si se puede" ("Yes we can" in Spanish), while drivers passing by honked their horns in celebration.

"It's a huge win for Texas, but it's a giant win for the United States, having James Talarico in the Senate to try to wrest control of this government that's out of control," said Kathy Jackoway, an Austin resident in her 60s.

"Everybody is suffering. Everybody is hurting, and Trump is busy building monuments to himself."

Anisha, 29, said she hoped the two Democrats would govern "for everyone, not just the billionaires, not just the elite."

The landmark victories for Democrats could signal that Texas, the country's second most populous state with 40 electoral votes, is becoming competitive in national elections, a shift that could reshape the electoral map for future races.

"This is a win the size of Texas and now we have a mandate the size of Texas," Talarico said.

The results mark a bruising defeat for Musk, who spent more than $200 million to support Talarico's rival, according to federal filings.

The world's richest man, Musk has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas.

The spread of AI data centers across Texas became a central issue in both races, as residents worried about rising electricity bills, water use and strain on the power grid.

Talarico and Hinojosa both called for tighter regulation, prompting Abbott, a longtime champion of the industry, to propose new rules of his own.

Talarico ran on a blend of Christian faith and economic populism, describing the contest as a David versus Goliath fight and inviting Republicans dissatisfied with the party to join him.

Trump traveled to Texas four times in the month before the election to rally for Paxton, whom he endorsed over four-term incumbent senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary.

Talarico, 37, was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2018 and built a national following with speeches combining progressive politics, biblical teaching and criticism of wealthy elites.

He defeated congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary and sought to broaden his appeal by criticizing aspects of former president Joe Biden's immigration policies.

Paxton, 63, survived impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on allegations of corruption and abuse of power before being acquitted by the state Senate. He has denied wrongdoing.

During the campaign, Talarico drew support from voters who had left the Republican Party, as well as from younger voters.

articles.title: Trump: Abbott would have won if he ‘hadn’t become a RINO’
articles.summary: President Trump blasted Texas Gov. Greg Abbott late Tuesday for losing his reelection bid, accusing the incumbent of being a “RINO,” or Republican in name only. “If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.…
articles.body:
President Trump blasted Texas Gov. Greg Abbott late Tuesday for losing his reelection bid , accusing the incumbent of being a “RINO,” or Republican in name only.

“If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!”

The three-term governor went down to defeat by a wide margin to his Democratic challenger, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected . Hinojosa led by 7.4 points as of Wednesday morning.

Had he won, Abbott would have been the longest-serving chief executive in the Lone Star State.

The Texas Republican oversaw a rapid expansion of the state’s population and economy as governor, which became a political issue for him in the campaign. Hinojosa often targeted him on the issue of data centers, which he later took a stricter stance on.

In August, Trump called it a “mistake” following Abbott’s announcement of a moratorium on new data center construction, pending a state audit.

On other issues, the governor has remained a staunch supporter of the president and the right. Throughout his campaign, he accused his Democratic rival of supporting Sharia law, a Muslim religious code, as well as open borders and gender surgeries for minors.

Abbott has also signed into law one of the strictest abortion bans in the country during his tenure.

The president has also called out other GOP lawmakers and pundits in the state as being RINOs, including former President George W. Bush’s White House adviser Karl Rove and outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R).

Trump ultimately backed Cornyn’s challenger , Ken Paxton, in the Senate primary. Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico by a strong margin Tuesday night.

And when Rove endorsed Democrat Jon Rosenthal in the race for Texas railroad commissioner against his controversial GOP opponent, the president tore into him on social media.

Democrats in Texas had not won a statewide race since the 1990s or swept the statewide races in a single election since the 1980s. That streak was broken Tuesday with every statewide Democrat prevailing by at least 4 points, according to DDHQ.

articles.title: 2028 begins now: It’s time for a rebirth of a principled Republican Party
articles.summary: The struggle for the soul of the Republican Party now moves to a new level.
articles.body:
Republicans just lost both houses of Congress in a massive defeat and real-time referendum on the failed policies of President Donald J. Trump. The American people have rejected the president’s policies, big government Republicanism, MAGA, America First and the failures of the current administration and Republican Congress.

The 2028 presidential election begins now. Trump will likely never again lead the Republican party in a general election. It is time to begin the debate about the future of a principled Republican party in the post-Trump era.

My organization, Our Republican Legacy, is dedicated to nominating and electing a legacy Republican president. As candidates come forward and begin their presidential campaigns, we will be looking to support one or more leaders who stand for our party’s traditional core principles.

We embrace five founding principles that guide our value system and must once again guide the future of the GOP.

First, is unity. Like President Abraham Lincoln, the first Republican president, we believe in the sanctity of preserving our union and democracy by uniting — not dividing – Americans.

The second is the Constitution. We support and defend the rule of law, including all of our individual freedoms and rights under the Constitution. We oppose the rise of authoritarianism and corruption that undermines the rule of law and exceeds the chief executive’s legal authority.

Third, fiscal responsibility. We support the swift return to responsible fiscal policy to protect and defend the full faith and credit of the United States government, which is under attack and threatened by unsustainable federal debt that exceeds our annual gross domestic product .

Fourth, free enterprise. We support — and as a nation need — a thriving domestic economy as well as a globally competitive economy based on market principles with sound regulation, full transparency and disclosure and a clear legal framework. We oppose senseless, destructive tariffs, which are regressive taxes that raise prices on consumers and lead to unnecessary trade wars that no nation wins.

Fifth and finally, peace through strength. Our society’s freedoms and resilience as an inspiring beacon of hope and democracy for other nations for over 250 years are supported by maintaining a strong national defense. We oppose a retreat into isolationism and launching unauthorized wars that lack popular support or a strategy for victory. We recommit to our traditional allies and strategic alliances such as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We support the defense of Ukraine against Russian aggression.

We call on all traditional Reaganite legacy conservatives who share these principles to rally and reengage, whether you have left the Republican Party, or have simply remained silent during the Trump years. We are confident that one or more strong conservative leaders will emerge in the presidential contest soon to begin. They will need our help.

The struggle for the soul of the Republican Party now moves to a new level. This battle will be waged on multiple fronts: grassroots conversations, party organizations, local contests, candidate recruitment, congressional and legislative primaries and ultimately the nomination of a true Republican for president.

This administration’s MAGA culture and its big government, divisive, protectionist, nativist and isolationist ideology must not be the future of the party of Abraham Lincoln, Teddy Roosevelt, Dwight Eisenhower and Ronald Reagan.

Political parties are defined by struggle and competition. Conservatives lost control of the Republican Party in 2016 to Trump’s band of populists. It is time for principled Republicans to take it back.

Chris Vance is executive director of Our Republican Legacy and a former chairman of the Washington State Republican Party.

articles.title: El-Sayed tells Sky News reporter he wants ‘zero’ votes in UK
articles.summary: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) got into a heated exchange with a British reporter on Election Day, questioning why he should answer questions from a journalist who was not registered to vote in Michigan. El-Sayed, who defeated Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers on Tuesday to become the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate, was…
articles.body:
Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) got into a heated exchange with a British reporter on Election Day, questioning why he should answer questions from a journalist who was not registered to vote in Michigan.

El-Sayed, who defeated Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers on Tuesday to become the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate, was approached by Sky News U.S. correspondent James Matthews, who sought to question the Democrat about the race.

“Are you registered to vote in the state of Michigan?” El-Sayed asked Matthews .

When Matthews said he was not, El-Sayed shot back, “Then why would I care to have a conversation with you?”

Matthews explained he was a journalist covering an election whose outcome “matters to the world,” but El-Sayed dismissed the argument.

“You know how many votes I want to get in the U.K.? Zero,” El-Sayed said. “I am never running for office in the U.K. … so I actually do not care what you think or the questions you ask.”

The exchange grew more tense as El-Sayed clapped his hands for emphasis and placed both hands on Matthews’s shoulders, and asked him to stop “chasing” him around.

“I am not chasing you around, I am asking you questions,” Matthews replied.

Video of the confrontation circulated on social media, drawing millions of views as well as criticism from several prominent British journalists.

British broadcaster Piers Morgan called El-Sayed’s behavior “pathetic” and “very patronising,” writing on the social platform X that the incoming senator “should allow more respect to the UK and one of our best journalists.”

Sky News special correspondent Alex Crawford defended Matthews, arguing that the outcome of American elections has implications well beyond the country’s borders.

“Bravo to our colleague @jamesmatthewsky for always asking the pertinent question and putting into context just why what happens in Michigan – and America – doesn’t stay in Michigan,” Crawford wrote on X . “The election most certainly matters elsewhere – and non-voters have a significance of their own.”

articles.body:
President Trump is seeking to blame Tuesday’s disastrous midterm election results for Republicans on Fox News, which he attacked repeatedly on social media before calling into the network on election night.

“Why does FoxNews have Bill de Blasio, the Worst Mayor in the History of New York City, on air, ranting and raving like a Lunatic,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform after de Blasio appeared on the network to analyze Tuesday’s election results. “He left the City in disgrace, and the damage he caused was incalculable — It has never been the same, and now he’s telling us how to run America. FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse.”

Trump later called into Fox and insisted that if he were on the ballot , Republicans would not have suffered the sweeping losses they were handed in states including Texas, Ohio and Maine.

Democrats notched resounding victories on Tuesday, winning control of the House and Senate and setting up a clash with Trump during the final two years of his presidency.

Trump’s attacks on Fox were consistent on election night, with the president calling out pundits by name and knocking polling put forth by the network before votes were counted.

The president has had a complicated relationship with the Rupert Murdoch-owned cable channel for years, hiring a slew of former hosts at the network to serve in his administration and blasting Fox’s editorial decisionmaking.

articles.body:
Democrats will control both the Senate and the House of Representatives come Jan. 3, 2027, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) says he will not run for GOP leader in the next Congress as Republicans prepare for life in the minority.

The exact extent of Democrats’ majorities remains to be determined as some key races are still undecided as of early Wednesday. But Democrats picked up most of this year’s high-profile contests across the country, including the Texas Senate and gubernatorial races, Kansas Senate race , Iowa Senate and gubernatorial races, Michigan Senate race , Georgia Senate and gubernatorial races, and Maine Senate race .

Decision Desk HQ projects that the Democrats will hold 258 seats in the U.S. House to the GOP’s 177, while their Senate projection currently stands at 55 Democrats to 45 Republicans.

President Trump congratulated Democrats on their victories in a call with CBS News, but was quick to emphasize that he “wasn’t on the ballot” and that if he was, “we would have won.” He also said Fox News “bears responsibility for these losses.”

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), now set to be chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee after Democrats’ Election Day sweep , warned Trump administration officials they need to “lawyer up.”

The two-word statement from Garcia may have been brief but comes after Democrats on the panel have launched a number of investigations into administration activities.

The investigation into the activities of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein has shared bipartisan support and is expected to continue, but Democrats on the panel have expressed a desire to speak with more Trump administration officials about their knowledge of his activities.

Democrats have also launched a number of probes on their own, including into the activities of the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency, and have demanded information about the activities of various immigration agencies.

articles.title: Iran weighs in on midterms: ‘Americans said NO TO WAR’
articles.summary: Iran’s top negotiator responded to the resounding Republican defeat in the midterm elections as proof of American voters rejecting President Trump’s war against his country and the associated economic burden. “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s Parliament who…
articles.body:
Iran’s top negotiator responded to the resounding Republican defeat in the midterm elections as proof of American voters rejecting President Trump’s war against his country and the associated economic burden.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s Parliament who is leading negotiations with the U.S., said on the social platform X .

He further threatened a “Nightmare” if Trump follows through on threats to return to open conflict.

“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he said.

Trump acknowledged the war with Iran “was a piece” of the backlash to Republican candidates, in an interview with The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday evening.

While American voters rated the war with Iran as a low priority among the issues they weighed going to the polls, they did connect their economic woes of high gas prices and inflation to the conflict. Affordability was the top issue for voters on Tuesday.

A Chicago Council on Foreign Affairs report released in September found about 86 percent of Americans broadly view the US-Iran war as bad for the cost of living in the country.

Ahead of and on election day, Trump played down resuming military operations against Iran even as the U.S. has continued to carry out limited strikes against the country, added to its armed presence in the region and had the Pentagon draw up strike options.

“I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it,” Trump said in an interview with the Financial Times on Tuesday.

Iranian officials have signaled that Tehran and Washington remain far apart on negotiations, with a senior Iranian official telling Reuters the U.S. must meet Iran’s conditions to open the Strait of Hormuz.

This includes waiving oil sanctions, ending the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds. Iran has strangled the waterway in retaliation for the U.S. war, impacting energy shipments through the strait that have sent energy prices skyrocketing around the world.

“Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington,” the senior Iranian official told Reuters.

articles.title: CEOs, get ready: Democratic oversight is coming for corporate America
articles.summary: Signs point to an exceptionally tough two years for business leaders, whom many on the left believe cowered under pressure from the president.
articles.body:
When the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027, Big Business could find itself in the crosshairs. Second only to administration officials, the Trump family itself and political operatives, corporate America may sit near the top of Democrats’ ambitious oversight agenda.

Signs point to an exceptionally tough two years for business leaders, whom many on the left believe cowered under pressure from the president.

And the implications for corporate America are consequential. Companies that cultivated cozy White House relationships , financed presidential initiatives, secured lucrative government contracts, or benefited from lax enforcement could soon find themselves in the hot seat during contentious congressional hearings.

Perhaps the sharpest questions will concern not what companies did, but why. Were public commitments quietly traded for access? Did boardrooms trade principle for profit? What did executives know, and when?

CEOs who think scrutiny will stop at political donors and Silicon Valley are missing a bigger picture. Banking, insurance, media, health care, transportation, energy, manufacturing and international trade are all fair targets for congressional investigations. As Dems seek to punish billionaires and high-profile business leaders for what they consider political profiteering, no industry should feel immune from the pent-up scorn of a party that has been shut out of power.

Nor should executives mistake divided government for congressional impotence. A Democratic House cannot enact its entire legislative agenda without the Senate and president, but it can demand documents, summon witnesses and conduct investigations within its jurisdiction. Subpoenas, document demands and other investigative tools can be just as troublesome — if not more — as adverse legislation or regulation. While legislation may die at the doorstep of the White House, an investigation can live on for months, sometimes years .

Should Democrats also capture the Senate, the stakes rise. Committees in both chambers could investigate the same company from different angles, while also advancing legislation on antitrust, finance, data privacy, labor and trade. Dual Democratic control would mean an aggressive and ambitious legislative agenda designed to make up for lost ground.

Imagine a CEO, under oath, being asked to justify an internal email about a government contract, a merger review or a private conversation with a high-ranking administration official. Edited for maximum media effect, broadcast on a 24-hour loop and presented as breaking news, this scenario portends a company’s biggest nightmare. The media’s appetite for political drama, real or manufactured, is bottomless, and a CEO twisting in the wind makes for great ratings.

K Street lawyers, lobbyists and consultants already see the commercial possibilities. For them, a congressional reckoning is a growth market: subpoena responses, document reviews, mock hearings, witness prep, negotiations with committee staff, crisis communications and the follow-on litigation that oversight tends to spawn. Their corporate clients, meanwhile, should prepare for a modern-day inquisition into their business practices and priorities over the last two years — and be prepared to pay handsomely for it.

Hearings, however, are only the beginning. Public spectacle has other, equally damaging, consequences in the market. Congressional scrutiny can rattle investors, embolden activists, invite shareholder lawsuits, stimulate state enforcement and provoke consumer backlash , even when accusations prove unfounded. The direct hit on stock prices, the market and corporate reputation is registered in real time, and could takes months to recover.

America’s banks should know. Debanking, consumer fees, credit availability, digital assets and their relationships with federal regulators already present thorny problems for them. Democrats could spotlight lending fairness, account closures, executive pay and alleged preferential treatment from Washington. Insurance companies are no less vulnerable . Rising premiums, disputed claims, coverage limitations, underwriting practices and executive compensation practically write their own hearing agendas.

Not to be overlooked, media and entertainment industries could face similar examination. Broadcast ownership, mega mergers, advertising practices, carriage disputes, streaming services and a deferential relationship with the administration and the Federal Communications Commission invite scrutiny. So do questions surrounding media censorship, the First Amendment and restrictions on press access to government.

But Big Tech may be the most conspicuous target . Executives who embraced the administration’s policies lock, stock and barrel may be asked about government contracts, regulatory favors, political contributions, and their influence over federal policy. Legitimate questions about privacy, competition, consumer protection and artificial intelligence deserve legitimate answers from Big Tech leaders.

Few issues have brought together such unlikely allies as the enormous AI facilities throughout the country. They have promised jobs and investment while prompting concerns about electricity rates, water use, land, tax incentives and community economic development. While both Democratic and Republican members have sought restrictions, moratoria and outright bans on new development, for congressional Democrats, data centers may be the low-hanging fruit they need to connect even more intimately with political independents.

Beyond the data center debate lie even larger questions about the integrity of America’s electric grid, personal privacy, job displacement, and global competition with China. Other industries should be on alert.

Transportation, energy, trade, and health care are also fair game for Democratic review. Airlines may face renewed questions about safety and service. Retailers could be pressed about tariffs, overseas sourcing and supply chains. Energy, oil and gas industries stand to answer questions on permits, pricing, the environment and profits. And the health care industry faces perennial questions about rising costs and shrinking coverage.

Corporate America should expect more than a change in committee leadership — it should expect a change in perspective. Issues involving Big Business, Big Tech and Big Banks are too consequential to the economy, too visible to the public and too rich in political opportunity to be left alone.

But there is a cautionary tale for Democrats as well.

Whether they control one house of Congress or two, Democrats must remember that punishing business is not the same as protecting the public. They can demand corporate accountability without declaring war on business. American companies employ millions of people, invest billions of dollars and compete in a global economy against foreign rivals determined to capture and control our markets. Congress should be mindful that political spectacle carries an economic price, and that price is rarely paid by CEOs alone. It falls on employees, shareholders, consumers and communities.

China, Russia and foreign competitors will not suspend their efforts and ambitions while Washington settles political scores. They will exploit every distraction, every delayed investment and every self-inflicted wound. Democrats should understand that Congress needs vigilance, not vengeance. American voters want accountability, not animosity, from its leaders.

Anything else is a dereliction of their duty to American citizens and the United States Constitution.

Adonis Hoffman writes on business, law and policy. He served in senior legal roles in the U.S. House of Representatives and at the Federal Communications Commission.

articles.title: Obama applauds Democratic sweep
articles.summary: Former President Obama applauded Democratic candidates for a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, with Democrats winning competitive races and taking control of the House and Senate. “Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to…
articles.body:
Former President Obama applauded Democratic candidates for a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, with Democrats winning competitive races and taking control of the House and Senate.

“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” Obama said in a post on the social platform X early Wednesday.

With big wins in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa, Michigan and Maine, the Democrats won a Senate majority and are on track to win 54 to 56 seats. The party also seized control of the House and is projected to win around 255 seats, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The Democratic wave in Texas was brought by the historic wins of candidates James Talarico and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D), who defeated their Republican opponents Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, respectively, in the state’s Senate and gubernatorial races .

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers, making history as the first Muslim American elected to the upper chamber. Democrat Adam Hamilton also flipped a Senate seat in Kansas and is going to be the first Democratic senator from the Sunflower State since 1939.

“These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country — including in areas once considered long shots,” Obama said in his post.

“They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first,” he added.

The midterm victory puts House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) in line to be the country’s first Black Speaker. The Speakership vote will take place on the House floor on Jan. 3.

In his message, the former president thanked election officials and volunteers who helped with running things smoothly on Tuesday. In the end, he set the tone for the next two years, saying, “Our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future.”

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are both expected to launch bids for minority leader, setting up a potentially contentious contest as Republicans grapple with their diminished standing .

Johnson has had a rocky tenure as Speaker, often marked by internal GOP fighting, a razor-thin margin and repeated challenges in keeping his conference united over government funding, the Iran war and other issues.

He was first elected to Congress in 2016, and he was elected as Speaker in 2023, succeeding former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.). Before taking on that role, he served as the vice chair of the House Republican Conference.

articles.title: Congress drafted a historic climate bill. Environmental groups want to kill it.
articles.summary: Environmental organizations are opposing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which aims to accelerate the U.S. clean energy transition by streamlining permitting processes and limiting litigation.
articles.body:
On Nov. 9, the Senate will take up the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act , a sweeping bill that could become one of America’s most powerful climate policies. Stunningly, environmental groups are lining up in opposition.

America’s clean energy transition is underway, but slow permitting, aging power lines, yearslong lawsuits, and White House interference have prevented solar and wind projects from being built and connected as quickly as the climate crisis demands. This bill could change that. It would streamline project approvals and grid connections, limit lawsuits that stall construction, and restrict presidential intrusion. It could help America accelerate the clean energy buildout necessary to lower electric bills and fight climate change.

Yet 222 environmental organizations, including Greenpeace USA, the Climate Justice Alliance, and the Center for Biological Diversity, signed a letter urging Congress to reject the bill, arguing its environmental cost would “outweigh the potential emissions reductions” it could deliver. That calculation dangerously undervalues the status quo’s climate cost. By rejecting limits on the ability to delay or derail development, environmentalists risk sacrificing the biggest opportunity in decades to advance a sustainable future.

Energy economics has fundamentally changed. Globally, 91 percent of renewables commissioned in 2024 were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives. Over the past decade, solar panel prices fell by 90 percent , onshore wind by 70 percent , and batteries by more than 90 percent . Unfortunately, developers spend years purchasing land, securing approvals, navigating environmental reviews and public comments, upgrading the grid, and fighting lawsuits before installing a single panel or turbine. Today’s challenge is no longer affording solar and wind, but whether our convoluted procedures allow them to be built.

The backlog is staggering: 773 gigawatts of solar capacity sat in America’s grid interconnection queues as of December, over two and a half times the solar capacity installed nationwide. Of proposals between 2016 and 2020, 11.3 percent of solar capacity in red states became operational, compared with 5.4 percent in blue states. Policy doesn’t tell the whole story — too many projects fail everywhere — but states with fewer bureaucratic hurdles get more proposed solar permitted and built than their climate-ambitious but high-regulation counterparts.

After developers secure permits and transmission upgrades, appeals challenging renewable projects can take over two years to resolve . Many stem from President Trump’s crusade against offshore wind , but environmental groups counterintuitively bring a substantial share of lawsuits themselves. Uncertainty forces developers to maintain land without revenue, making promising renewable projects uneconomical while Americans burn far worse fossil fuels instead.

The bill could dramatically improve this. Federally, it would impose permitting deadlines, coordinate grid upgrades, and give regulators greater authority to approve interstate power lines. Lawsuits challenging federal environmental reviews would generally face a 150-day filing deadline , with stricter guidelines for courts overturning approvals. Crucially, the bill would prevent presidents from revoking permits or targeting energy sources for political reasons, as Trump has repeatedly attempted with wind.

Knowing this, one might expect environmental organizations to be the legislation’s fiercest champions. Instead, many are its fiercest opponents.

Many environmentalists object that the bill would ease fossil fuel permitting, a concession they consider untenable. But today’s infrastructure barriers don’t displace fossil fuels; they entrench them as the only option. Reform won’t fix that alone, but with solar, onshore wind, and battery storage comprising 93 percent of planned 2026 U.S. electricity additions, clean energy is better positioned to capitalize on deregulatory policy. American Clean Power projects the bill could avert 290 million metric tons of carbon emissions annually, a 6 percent reduction. The faster we build clean energy, the more it can meet America’s growing electricity demand, letting us retire fossil fuels without harming people’s energy bills and lifestyles.

The letter also argues reforming environmental laws would cause damage outweighing these emissions cuts. That may be defensible for specific provisions, and legislators should seek amendments, particularly on tribal sovereignty and judicial remedies . But measured against the status quo, fossil fuel extraction and worsening climate change threaten our air, water, and ecosystems far more than an accelerated-but-still-lawful clean energy buildout. Speed matters in climate mitigation. Competing environmental concerns cannot keep taking years to raise and evaluate.

The groups also claim “now is not the right moment” for compromise and a future Democratic Congress could deliver a preferable package. That’s a terrifying gamble. This polarized Congress has passed no discretionary bipartisan reforms of comparable scope. Its closest bipartisan success, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, went unsigned by the president . Nevertheless, the unpredictable White House seems open to permitting reform . If Democrats bail, they risk politicizing future reform under a president willing to reject popular bipartisan legislation to punish Democrats. The Inflation Reduction Act fallout revealed waiting for one-party trifectas and legislating alone won’t produce stable climate policy . This legislation may not satisfy every environmentalist’s wish list, but squashing a rare bipartisan chance to reform 50-year-old laws for the century’s most urgent environmental challenge because it’s “not the right moment” is incredibly misguided.

For decades, environmentalists have notched victories blocking destructive development and protecting natural spaces. But those efforts were never ends in themselves. They envisioned a better future: cleaner air and water, thriving communities, and prosperity without sacrificing the planet. Today, realizing that future requires green infrastructure to replace fossil fuels, mitigate climate change, and lower electric bills. This bill offers a historic opportunity to build that. By fighting it, environmental organizations risk jeopardizing the vision they’ve spent decades imagining. I hope they reconsider.

Ethan Brown is Program Manager at the University of Rhode Island’s Metcalf Institute. He is an award-winning climate writer and commentator with a B.A. in Environmental Analysis & Policy from Boston University. His opinions are his own. Click here to follow his work.

Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., talk to reporters about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to reform the federal environmental review and permitting process, at the Capitol in Washington, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. articles.body:
Democrat Aaron Ford is projected to defeat Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) in the Nevada governor’s race, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Ford, the Nevada attorney general, defeated first-term Lombardo to be Nevada’s top executive. Lombardo’s loss underscores the Democratic blue wave that’s splashed across the nation where even more reliably Republican areas like Texas and Kansas have fallen to the Democrats.

Lombardo’s loss is particularly notable given he was the one Republican to flip a Democratic-held governorship in 2022, serving a bright spot for the party in an otherwise red ripple of a midterm year for the GOP.

Ford tied the Nevada governor to President Trump as Democrats throughout the country nationalized the race and tied vulnerable GOP incumbents to a president whose approval ratings have sharply declined. The Nevada Democrat also leaned into issues such as adding more affordable housing in the state and repealing the state’s “right-to-work” law.

Lombardo and Republicans sought to attack Ford, particularly for his multiple trips out of the state and for his track on issues such as crime.

Ford’s win is historic, making him the first Black governor to helm the Silver State.

articles.title: Democrats clinch open Amodei House seat in Nevada
articles.summary: Democrats are projected to flip retiring Rep. Mark Amodei’s (R) seat in northern Nevada, per Decision Desk HQ. Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson, a social worker and former majority leader of the state House, defeated Republican David Flippo, an Air Force veteran, to clinch the district that encompasses Reno and the entire upper half of the Silver…
articles.body:
Democrats are projected to flip retiring Rep. Mark Amodei’s (R) seat in northern Nevada, per Decision Desk HQ.

Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson, a social worker and former majority leader of the state House, defeated Republican David Flippo, an Air Force veteran, to clinch the district that encompasses Reno and the entire upper half of the Silver State.

She notched more than 50 percent of the vote while the Republican garnered just more than 44 percent, with 85 percent of the vote tallied Wednesday morning.

Benitez-Thompson’s victory delivers a major blow to Republicans in a conservative stronghold that’s never sent a Democrat to Congress. President Trump carried the 2nd District by 14 percentage points in 2024.

The Republican candidate has faced allegations of financial wrongdoing. And late in the campaign it was revealed that he had falsely claimed for years that he earned a Bronze Star award “with valor,” meaning he performed acts of heroism in combat. In fact, he received a Bronze Star in 2004, but not for valor.

Amodei has called Flippo a “fraud” and said he wouldn’t vote for him.

Flippo’s campaign said the distortion was the result of “honest mistakes” made by aides. But the scandals dogged Flippo’s campaign and gave hope to Democrats that Benitez-Thompson could flip the seat.

House Democrats’ campaign arm included the Nevada contest on its coveted “Red to Blue” list, and Benitez-Thompson notched endorsements from key Democrats , including Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego and California Rep. Pete Aguilar.

Her campaign largely focused on affordability, fighting corruption in Washington and protecting public lands.

articles.title: North Carolina Democrat Ojeda defeats NRCC Chair Richard Hudson in House race

Hudson’s role as the NRCC chair meant he was tasked with helping protect vulnerable House Republicans across the…
articles.body:
Democrat Richard Ojeda is projected to defeat Rep. Richard Hudson (R), the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC), in the race for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ.

Hudson’s role as the NRCC chair meant he was tasked with helping protect vulnerable House Republicans across the country and had to devote some resources toward his own reelection campaign, according to Cook Political Report .

The Democrat eked out a victory with more than 51 percent support, with 95 percent of the vote tallied. The incumbent garnered nearly 49 percent of the vote.

Democratic operatives were skeptical of Ojeda’s ability to close the gap in his challenge against Hudson, Cook Political Report stated. The race shifted Sunday from being a solidly Republican district to being a likely Republican win.

The 9th Congressional District is home to Hoke, Moore, Randolph and Alamance counties, along with portions of Guilford, Cumberland and Chatham counties, including part of the city of Greensboro.

Ojeda’s victory marks the first Democratic win in the district since 1963. He ran a campaign focused on ousting Hudson, who Ojeda’s campaign website says “voted to make life more expensive for working families, from utilities to electricity costs.”

“He’s running for Congress because he’s sick of politicians getting richer while working people get sold out,” Ojeda’s website states. “In Congress, he’ll secure the border, and take on the rigged system and corrupt politicians by making billionaires and corporations pay their fair share and banning members of Congress from trading stocks.”

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee launched TV ads going after Hudson in the few days before the election, with Ojeda telling voters the rising cost of healthcare and contributions to Hudson’s campaign from the pharmaceutical industry made things “a corrupt mess,” The Carolina Journal reported.

articles.title: Wall Street Journal editorial board: Trump ‘main architect’ of GOP midterm ‘rout’
articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board cast much of the blame on President Trump for GOP losses Tuesday, as Democrats are poised to take control of both the House and Senate. “Republicans may console themselves that midterm defeats in second presidential terms are common. But this was more than a normal defeat,” the board wrote…
articles.body:
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board cast much of the blame on President Trump for GOP losses Tuesday, as Democrats are poised to take control of both the House and Senate.

“Republicans may console themselves that midterm defeats in second presidential terms are common. But this was more than a normal defeat,” the board wrote in a piece published early Wednesday.

“The loss of Senate seats and governorships in states that had become GOP redoubts will have ramifications for years to come,” it continued. “So will the cascading losses down ballot in state legislatures.”

“True to form, President Trump is already blaming everyone else, but he is the main architect of this rout,” the board added.

Trump has taken his frustration over the results out on the media and GOP candidates he accused of being “Republican in Name Only.” The Journal suggested the president could also look at the Senate filibuster and lack of action on his Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act — which would require proof of citizenship to vote if passed — as fodder for the upsets.

“But neither would have saved the GOP this year, even if there had been enough votes to do either,” the Journal piece reads.

A blue wave cascaded throughout the U.S. on Tuesday, locking down the possibility of limiting Trump’s power through his last two years in office.

The Democratic victories came as the GOP faced rocky political territory over issues including the unpopular war in Iran , Trump’s slumping approval numbers and concerns about the cost of living.

Democrats are projected to secure 256 seats in the House and 55 seats in the Senate, according to Decision Desk HQ, marking gains for the party that currently holds 214 seats in the lower chamber and 45 seats in the upper. It’s a notable victory for a party that was marred by infighting and frustration in the wake of their 2024 election losses.

“More broadly, the President’s erratic and self-indulgent second-term governance has alienated much of the coalition he assembled in 2024. He won a second term on the promise to repeat the economic success of his first,” the Journal’s board wrote.

“But this time he insisted on imposing universal tariffs, often willy-nilly, that have raised prices for many goods and been especially damaging in Iowa, Kansas and the Farm Belt,” it added. “His senseless trade war with Canada hurt Republicans in Michigan, Maine, even Texas.”

When reached for comment, a White House official told The Hill that “The White House mood is defiant.”

“President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot.”

articles.title: Idaho voters choose an official state gun
articles.summary: Idaho voters overwhelmingly supported the Winchester Model 1873 rifle as the official state gun over five other guns. The rifle garnered around 31 percent of the vote as of early Wednesday morning, with the Winchester Model 1894 at around 25 percent, according to The Associated Press. The Winchester Model 1873 was the focus of the…
articles.body:
Idaho voters overwhelmingly supported the Winchester Model 1873 rifle as the official state gun over five other guns.

The rifle garnered around 31 percent of the vote as of early Wednesday morning, with the Winchester Model 1894 at around 25 percent, according to The Associated Press .

The Winchester Model 1873 was the focus of the 1955 film “The Gun that Won the West,” and Buffalo Bill — a famous figure in the Old West — declared that it was “The Boss,” according to Field & Stream .

The National Park Service stated it was majorly popularized as “everyman’s” rifle, noting that 720,610 were manufactured between 1873 and 1916, when production ended. It was developed in New Haven, Conn.

The Idaho advisory, which pitted six guns against one another, was to commemorate the U.S.’s 250th anniversary, state legislators said. The legislation that proposed the advisory cited the country’s long history with guns, including “citizen militias” arming themselves “with long rifles in the Revolutionary War to secure liberty.”

“In Idaho, explorers, such as Meriwether Lewis and William Clark in 1805 through 1806, depended on rifles for survival while crossing Idaho’s wilderness, hunting game and protecting against dangers,” it continued.

The vote is nonbinding in Idaho, as state lawmakers still have to consider legislation to formally designate the voters’ choice in a 2027 legislative session.

Eleven other states have selected a state gun in the last 15 years, with Utah and Arizona being the first to adopt their choices in 2011. Utah picked the Browning M1911 , which was designed by Utah native John Browning, while Arizona chose the Colt Single Action Army revolver, also known as the “Peacemaker.”

The “Peacemaker,” the Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle, Colt M1911 and M1 Garand rifle were the other options for Idaho voters.

articles.title: Peltola takes slight lead in Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola has taken a slight lead in Alaska’s Senate race by about 500 votes, results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) show, putting a possible eighth flip in the Senate in reach. As of almost 11 a.m. Wednesday, Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) with 48.2 percent to his 47.9 percent with 70 percent…
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola has taken a slight lead in Alaska’s Senate race by about 500 votes, results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) show , putting a possible eighth flip in the Senate in reach.

As of almost 11 a.m. Wednesday, Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) with 48.2 percent to his 47.9 percent with 70 percent of the expected vote counted.

Alaska does not have counties, instead separating its votes by state house district. DDHQ shows that Peltola is exceeding her “benchmarks” — the estimated result she would need to be on track to win statewide — in 26 out of 40 state house districts. Sullivan is exceeding his marks in the other 14, DDHQ shows.

Peltola now leads in a majority of state house districts, at 24. The outstanding vote also suggests that the former congresswoman may have more room to grow her lead — districts where she is ahead are averaging 68.6 percent of the expected vote reported, while districts where Sullivan is ahead are averaging 73.2 percent of the expected vote reported.

Still, if neither candidate reaches 50 percent, Alaska will proceed with an instant runoff using its ranked choice voting (RCV) system. RCV will tally up voters’ second, third and fourth place votes, if they ranked all candidates, and add to the remaining candidates’ vote shares until one candidate has the majority.

But that process cannot happen until all voters are counted and processed in Alaska. Given the rural and expansive nature of the state, ballots have 15 days after the election to arrive.

A proposition to repeal RCV was on this year’s ballot in Alaska, and it is losing by a nearly 4-point margin, according to DDHQ.

Alaska will not report more votes until Nov. 10, when most remaining early and mail ballots will be counted, according to nonpartisan election news site Votebeat. The final votes will be included in the count on Nov. 18, when the state will run RCV if necessary.

A win for Democrats in Alaska was once thought to be a necessity for the party to win back control of the Senate. Now, it would just be one more seat.

Democrats already picked up seven Senate seats, DDHQ projections show, with Alaska and Mississippi still outstanding. The gains were part of a big night for Democrats nationally in which they reclaimed control of Congress with healthy margins.

articles.title: First Democrat wins statewide office in Indiana since 2012
articles.summary: Democrat Beau Bayh pulled off a major upset in Indiana’s secretary of state race Tuesday, becoming the first Democrat to win statewide office in the Republican stronghold in more than a decade. Bayh defeated Republican Max Engling in a closely watched contest that drew national attention as Democrats sought to break the GOP’s grip on…
articles.body:
Democrat Beau Bayh pulled off a major upset in Indiana’s secretary of state race Tuesday, becoming the first Democrat to win statewide office in the Republican stronghold in more than a decade.

Bayh defeated Republican Max Engling in a closely watched contest that drew national attention as Democrats sought to break the GOP’s grip on statewide elections. Engling conceded around 11:30 p.m., and Bayh led with 51.7 percent of the vote to Engling’s 42.6 percent, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The victory marks a significant breakthrough for Indiana Democrats, who have not won a statewide election since 2012, and comes after a turbulent campaign to replace outgoing Secretary of State Diego Morales (R).

“Today, Hoosiers voted for change,” Bayh, the son of former Sen. Evan Bayh (D-Ind.), told supporters gathered at a hotel in downtown Indianapolis.

“For too long, the people of our state have taken for granted, too many decisions have been made behind closed doors by insiders,” he said. “Too many families have played by the rules while the people in the halls of power played by indifference.”

He continued, “Tonight we said enough is enough.”

Bayh ran a campaign focused on winning over moderate and conservative voters, emphasizing his military background and promising to bring greater accountability to the secretary of state’s office.

His appeal appeared to extend beyond traditional Democratic strongholds. Bayh led in Marion and Lake counties, home to large Democratic voting blocs, while also making inroads in Republican-leaning areas of central and southern Indiana, including counties that overwhelmingly backed President Trump in 2024.

The race had become an unexpected battleground after Morales, the incumbent Republican secretary of state, was denied renomination at the state GOP convention in June following a series of controversies surrounding his tenure.

Engling ultimately secured the Republican nomination but faced a crowded general election field that included former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard, who ran under the newly formed Lincoln Party banner, and Libertarian Lauri Shillings.

Engling conceded Tuesday night at a Republican watch party in Indianapolis.

“The voters have made their decision and it’s not what we wanted,” he told supporters, adding that he wished Bayh “success for the good of all Hoosiers in Indiana.”

articles.title: Jim Jordan announces he will run for minority leader, teeing up fight with Scalise
articles.summary: House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) announced Wednesday that he will run for minority leader, formally entering the race to lead House Republicans in the next Congress after they suffered a major blow in the midterms. He will likely face a contentious fight against current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.). Speaker Mike Johnson…
articles.body:
House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) announced Wednesday that he will run for minority leader, formally entering the race to lead House Republicans in the next Congress after they suffered a major blow in the midterms.

He will likely face a contentious fight against current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.).

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said on a staff call Wednesday that he will not run for minority leader, according to two GOP staffers.

Jordan wrote in a letter to his Republican colleagues on Wednesday that “for too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us.”

“That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority,” he wrote, adding that he is “battle-tested on the oversight front” and “I know the Democrats’ playbook.”

“I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics. We need a Leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight shooting,” Jordan wrote.

A key Trump ally, Jordan serves as the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, a perch he’s used over the last several years to investigate President Trump’s political opponents and Democratic officials and more notably referred former Special Counsel Jack Smith to the Department of Justice for criminal prosecution this year.

Jordan was set to lose his post leading the House Judiciary Committee regardless of the election’s outcome. He’s termed out on the panel, prompting inquiries about whether he might also seek to return to the House Oversight Committee, a panel he also previously chaired and which is also losing its GOP leader, as Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) won his bid for governor.

He is also a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, a far-right conservative group that has often butted heads with GOP leadership on government spending, and served as its first chairman in 2015. He could attract support from hardliners, many of whom have repeatedly clashed with Johnson and blocked legislation from advancing.

Jordan previously ran for Speaker in 2023, but failed to garner enough support to secure the gavel.

He has demonstrated loyalty to Trump on a number of fronts. During the Biden administration, he demanded Smith as well as top prosecutors in New York and Georgia turn over information about their criminal investigations into the president’s role on Jan. 6.

He also reversed his long-held position on warrantless spy powers earlier this year when Trump called for renewing the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act without significant reforms.
